W7214118204.abstract: Animal diseases continuously threaten livestock production and public health, yet current surveillance approaches remain largely passive and fragmented. Conventional artificial intelligence models typically function as open-loop predictors, delivering static outputs that fail to accommodate the dynamic operational needs of veterinarians in real-world farm settings. This review explores an emerging paradigm of AI agents for animal disease monitoring, emphasizing how such agents can transition from passive observation to active intervention through a closed-loop perception-decision-feedback architecture. We first classify multi-scale sensing technologies: at the micro-scale, automated molecular diagnostics and biosensors; at the macro-scale, computer-vision-based phenotyping. These technologies collectively provide the data streams required for continuous surveillance. The review then discusses how multi-modal inputs, time-series forecasting, resource-aware decision-making, and reinforcement learning can be integrated into an agent-based workflow. Importantly, most current veterinary research evidence supports only the individual components of this framework, rather than the deployment of fully autonomous, iteratively evolving closed-loop agents in actual field environments. Translating closed-loop AI from a conceptual framework into a reliable veterinary decision-support tool will therefore require further advances in validation, standardization, governance, and human oversight.

W7214246236.abstract: Analog circuit sizing remains a challenging and time-consuming task due to the large design space, strong performance trade-offs, and increasing circuit complexity in scaled technologies. Although recent large language model (LLM)-based methods show promise in improving sample efficiency and interpretability, existing approaches often lack explicit circuit-topology understanding and are mainly evaluated on relatively simple analog building blocks. This paper presents a multi-agent LLM-based framework for complex analog circuit sizing. The proposed framework first analyzes the circuit topology and decomposes the netlist into functional blocks and substructures. It also extracts lightweight design knowledge for reuse. Based on the extracted topology and knowledge, a planner coordinates multiple role-specialized sizing agents to update design variables and achieve global performance specifications. This workflow mimics the collaborative process of an expert analog design team and provides a structured, interpretable, and simulation-driven optimization procedure. The framework was validated on eight circuits, with the largest design containing up to 55 transistors and 60 sizing variables. Notably, for the LDO benchmark, the proposed method achieved a 60\% success rate with an average of 83 iterations, where classical optimizers failed to find feasible solutions. Further, ablation studies demonstrate that topology understanding, design-knowledge infusion, and agent specialization provide complementary benefits. The source code is available to support reproducibility.

W7214358173.abstract: DNA sequencing pipelines, spanning quality control, alignment, variant calling, and annotation, are now reliably executed by workflow management systems that orchestrate established bioinformatics tools at scale. What remains manual is the decision layer surrounding that execution: selecting quality thresholds appropriate to a sample and platform, adjudicating borderline variant calls, diagnosing anomalies, and determining which findings warrant expert review. These decisions are repetitive, judgment-intensive, inconsistent across operators, and frequently undocumented. This paper introduces BaseCamp, a novel agentic AI framework for automating the decision layer of DNA sequencing pipelines. The framework decomposes the pipeline into six specialized AI agents, covering sample intake and quality control, alignment, variant calling, annotation, cross-stage monitoring, and reporting. Critically, BaseCamp agents do not perform sequence analysis: established tools execute alignment, calling, and annotation, while the agents select among them, configure them, interpret their output, and decide what follows. This confines language model reasoning to the judgment layer where it is reliable and preserves the reproducibility existing tooling guarantees. Agent reasoning is powered by a consortium of fine-tuned, domain-specialized large language models coordinated by a central reasoning LLM, executing locally so no sequencing data leaves the operating environment, under human-in-the-loop orchestration. Evaluation shows agent-generated configurations are concordant with expert practice, that an explicit filtering ledger renders inspectable what filtering otherwise removes without trace, and that cross-stage anomaly detection surfaces conditions execution monitoring misses. BaseCamp offers a generalizable blueprint for agentic automation of scientific data pipelines.

W7214370798.abstract: Self-assembled monolayers (SAMs) have become indispensable hole-transport layers in inverted perovskite solar cells which enables power conversion efficiencies (PCEs) above 27% in single-junction devices and above 32% in tandems where the tandem devices benefit disproportionately from SAM engineering with certified efficiencies exceeding 31%. In the review eight hypotheses have been proposed including the prediction that bisphosphonic acid SAMs will outperform monophosphonic acid SAMs in thermal stability, glycol ether side chains will improve both PCE and stability and machine learning can identify new SAMs with >27% PCE and >90% retention at 1000 h , the studied researches shows that carbazole-based SAMs with phosphonic acid anchoring groups dominate the field with Me-4PACz and MeO-2PACz . Co-SAM strategies that have hydrogen-bonding additives consistently improve PCE by (1–3)% absolute over single-component SAMs and that bisphosphonic acid anchoring groups are emerging as a way to improve thermal and damp heat stability. Operational stability under maximum power point tracking now exceeds 1000 h for optimized SAM systems though ISOS protocol adoption remains inconsistent.

W7214506743.abstract: Abstract Objective To systematically review the methods, validation frameworks, applications and regulatory landscape of synthetic data generation in healthcare, with a specific focus on rheumatology. Methods We searched PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase and arXiv (January 2016–January 2026). From 1099 database records and 7 expert-identified studies, 701 remained after removing 405 duplicates. Title and abstract screening excluded 353 records; full-text assessment of 348 articles excluded 120 (E1: n = 62; E2: n = 1; E3: n = 23; E4: n = 34), yielding 228 studies. Quality assessment of 13 rheumatology-specific studies using a 10-item checklist revealed 1 high-quality, 8 moderate-quality, and 4 low-quality studies, with systematic gaps in privacy evaluation (2/13) and reproducibility (1/13). Results The 228 included studies encompassed six generation-method categories (generative adversarial networks, diffusion models, large language models, statistical methods, rule-based simulators and hybrid approaches) and five thematic categories (digital twins, privacy-preserving methods, reviews, validation frameworks and healthcare applications), detailed in the supplementary methods. Validation remained inconsistent, with only a minority evaluating fidelity, utility and privacy simultaneously. In rheumatology, 13 studies spanned rheumatoid arthritis (n = 3), osteoarthritis (n = 3), Sjogren’s syndrome (n = 2), systemic sclerosis (n = 2), systemic lupus erythematosus (n = 2) and ankylosing spondylitis (n = 1). Only 2 of 13 formally evaluated privacy and only 1 shared code for reproducibility. Conclusion Synthetic data hold substantial promise for rheumatology, particularly for augmenting small cohorts in low-prevalence diseases, enabling privacy-preserving registry sharing and simulating clinical trial populations. Realizing this potential requires standardized validation, greater attention to privacy and reproducibility and regulatory clarity on synthetic health data.

W7214545571.abstract: Background: Laboratory medicine is transitioning from passive machine learning models and static decision-support algorithms toward agentic artificial intelligence (AI)—systems capable of goal-directed autonomy, environmental perception, multi-step reasoning, dynamic tool utilization, and iterative self-correction. This review synthesizes the operational frameworks and clinical implications of agentic AI across anatomical pathology and clinical laboratories (Biochemistry, hematology, microbiology, and molecular diagnostics). In anatomical pathology, multi-agent frameworks optimize whole-slide imaging workflows through adaptive region-of-interest navigation, autonomous pre-screening, automated biomarker quantification, and integrated multi-modal report generation. In clinical laboratories, agentic architectures streamline pre-analytic specimen quality verification, orchestrate real-time delta-check evaluations, resolve atypical hematologic cell flagging, guide microbiology culture plate selection, and automate complex next-generation sequencing variant curation. By interconnecting Laboratory Information Systems, digital instrumentation, and electronic health records, multi-agent networks bridge data silos to enable cross-disciplinary diagnostic synthesis. Despite substantial gains in diagnostic throughput, turnaround times, and quality assurance, clinical implementation is constrained by computational overhead, potential error propagation in reasoning chains, data privacy, and the risk of automated "hallucinations". Addressing these challenges necessitates robust human-in-the-loop oversight, standardized audit trails for decision chains, and evolving regulatory compliance frameworks (FDA, CE-IVDR). Agentic AI represents a paradigm shift from narrow analytical tools to collaborative diagnostic teammates, positioned to elevate precision medicine and operational efficiency while redefining the roles of pathologists and laboratory scientists.

W7214627046.abstract: Language agents struggle to act and learn in environments that require long sequences of low-level actions. Code-based abstractions can make these agents more productive by letting them invoke reusable skills instead of repeatedly selecting individual actions. The code handles recurring local decisions, while the language model decides which skills to use and how to combine them. Yet abstractions are leaky, and situations beyond a skill's capabilities may require a return to primitive actions. Motivated by this tradeoff between productivity and flexibility, we systematically study how code-based action abstraction affects the performance, inference cost, and learning of language agents. We study this in NetHack, a challenging, long-horizon game environment, using CodeHack, our library of code-based skills with natural-language descriptions. We use this library to compare agents restricted to primitives with those using semantic skills alone or in combination with primitives. We evaluate these agents in three settings: zero-shot prompting, supervised fine-tuning, and reinforcement learning. Across a broad zero-shot evaluation on NetHack, we find that compared with primitives, skills nearly triple game progression, while reducing inference cost per episode by 86%. Combining skills with primitives retains much of this benefit while preserving a path back down to low-level actions. Finally, in RL, we find that skill-based agents learn significantly faster than agents acting on primitives, achieving a 7.2x larger average gain in dungeon level over the same training budget. These results show that a supplied skill library can improve performance, efficiency, and learning, while retaining primitives provides flexibility when the library is insufficient. We release CodeHack together with training and evaluation code.

W7214636713.abstract: Liquid biopsy has emerged as an important minimally invasive technology in contemporary oncology, enabling repeated assessment of tumor-derived molecular information through blood and other biological fluids. Circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA), circulating tumor cells, cell-free DNA methylation patterns, extracellular vesicles, circulating RNA and fragmentomic signatures may provide dynamic information about tumor burden, treatment response, molecular residual disease and cancer recurrence. However, liquid biopsy generates complex, multidimensional datasets in which tumor-derived signals may be extremely small relative to biological and technical background. Artificial intelligence (AI), including machine learning and deep learning, offers a potential computational framework for integrating these heterogeneous signals and generating clinically meaningful predictions. This review examines the emerging convergence of AI and liquid biopsy, with particular emphasis on longitudinal cancer monitoring rather than cancer detection alone. The available PubMed-indexed literature was reviewed to evaluate the potential role of AI-enhanced liquid biopsy in treatment-response assessment, minimal residual disease detection, prediction of treatment resistance and early identification of disease recurrence. Evidence from colorectal, lung, breast, hepatocellular and other solid tumors is discussed. The review also addresses major translational barriers, including low tumor shedding, clonal hematopoiesis, analytical heterogeneity, external validation, algorithmic bias, interpretability, data privacy, cost and uncertainty regarding clinical actionability. Current evidence indicates that AI can extract complementary biological information from complex circulating biomarker datasets, but prospective validation is still required before widespread implementation. AI-enhanced liquid biopsy may ultimately support a transition from episodic, imaging-centered surveillance toward personalized, dynamic and molecularly informed cancer monitoring.

W7214661256.abstract: Semantic 3D city models offer rich urban information yet remain largely inaccessible to non-expert users due to their complex schemas, deep class hierarchies, and heterogeneous data structures. Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in natural language understanding and code generation. But applying them to domain-specific databases requires contextual knowledge that far exceeds what can be manually written and maintained. This paper presents a framework that automatically generates domain context from CityGML data stored in 3DCityDB instances. The framework decomposes domain knowledge into static components (database schema, query patterns, spatial capabilities) and dynamic components (available object classes, properties and generic attribute classifications). These components are assembled into a structured context representation served via the Model Context Protocol (MCP), forming a shared knowledge layer that most AI agents can consume. We evaluate the framework against five CityGML datasets from different countries where attribute values are given in different languages, levels of detail, and thematic modules. Results demonstrate that the system enables an LLM-based agent to correctly formulate complex SQL queries (including 3D spatial operations, multi-level feature relationships, and nested property access). Beyond querying, the generated context supports the creation of additional domain-specific agents for tasks such as semantic enrichment, data quality assessment, and urban scenario analysis, making the MCP Server a reusable domain knowledge interface for semantic 3D city models.

W7214708255.abstract: As optical networks continue to expand in scale, complexity, and service diversity, the implementation of automation has become essential for ensuring agility, efficiency, and reliability in the lifecycle management (LCM) of optical networks. Large language model (LLM) agents, distinguished by their progressively sophisticated capabilities in logical reasoning, adaptive decision-making, complex problem solving, and multi-task orchestration, present great opportunities to advance network automation beyond traditional AI techniques. Nevertheless, the application of LLM agents in optical networks remains in its early exploratory stage, challenged by the lack of multi-task coordination, high computational demands, data dependence, and reliability concerns. In this paper, we envision a conceptual roadmap toward agentic optical networks (AONs) by integrating LLM agents throughout LCM with high-level autonomy. First, we trace the evolution from manual operations to AI-empowered frameworks and distill key technologies in agents, providing actionable insights into leveraging its strengths for addressing practical network automation challenges. A core contribution of this paper is the proposal of a hierarchical multi-agent framework, which is specifically developed to manage every phase in the LCM of AONs, including planning, deployment, operation, maintenance, upgrade, and decommissioning, thereby enabling more cohesive and comprehensive automation throughout the entire lifecycle. In addition, future directions and underlying challenges are also discussed at the intersection of LLMs and optical networks. By aligning the LLM agent with the specialized requirements of AONs, this work aims to explore the potential for the evolution of optical networks moving from task-level semi-automatic execution toward lifecycle-level full autonomy.

W7214781948.abstract: Background and Objective: -VASc) score is fundamental for assessing thromboembolic risk in atrial fibrillation (AF). However, its limitations arise from relying solely on clinical parameters, without considering individual cardiac structural and functional changes. This review aims to explore the development and implementation of multimodal risk prediction models that integrate echocardiographic parameters with clinical data and biomarkers to achieve a more precise and individualized risk assessment. Methods: A comprehensive literature search was conducted using relevant electronic databases (e.g., PubMed, Web of Science and Embase) to identify studies focusing on echocardiographic parameters, AF, and thromboembolic risk prediction models published up to May 2026. Key Content and Findings: Echocardiographic parameters evaluating the left atrium and left atrial appendage (LAA; size, function, and morphology) have emerged as significant predictors of both prevalent thrombus formation and future thromboembolic events. This review details these key parameters and critically assesses various multimodal approaches, including those combining clinical-echocardiographic scores with artificial intelligence (AI) techniques. Importantly, these models demonstrate enhanced predictive accuracy for specific clinical endpoints over traditional clinical scores. Conclusions: Utilizing a multimodal approach provides a promising supplementary tool for refined risk assessment, rather than replacing guideline-based anticoagulation decisions. Future directions should focus on standardizing echocardiographic measurements, expanding the use of AI for automated analysis, and conducting prospective interventional trials to confirm clinical benefit.

W7214803785.abstract: Morphological ambiguity constitutes a significant challenge for natural language processing in agglutinative languages, as a single word form might include many grammatical categories. The Kazakh language features productive suffixation, vowel harmony, and intricate morphophonological patterns, which considerably hinder automatic morphological analysis. This work presents a transformer-based methodology for morphological disambiguation in Kazakh texts, with the objective of identifying the appropriate morphological interpretation of word forms within context. A contextual language model tailored for Kazakh is refined for token-level morphological tagging utilizing a manually validated annotated corpus of news articles. The suggested method utilizes self-attention mechanisms to capture long-range contextual dependencies that are challenging to represent with conventional rule­based or recurrent neural techniques. The experimental assessment reveals that the transformer-based model attains superior accuracy and F1-score relative to rule-based morphological analyzers and BiLSTM-based benchmarks. The findings demonstrate that contextualized embeddings significantly enhance the resolution of morphological ambiguity, especially with homonymous suffixes and infrequent grammatical structures. The results validate the efficacy of transformer topologies for low-resource agglutinative languages and establish a feasible basis for incorporating morphology-aware models into comprehensive Kazakh natural language processing frameworks.

W7215030624.abstract: Large Language Model (LLM) agents are increasingly deployed as populations of interacting entities, in which consensus --agreement on a shared answer-- emerges as a collective, unengineered behaviour. Prior work on LLM consensus shows that agents can cross-verify their answers and converge towards more factual responses, treating agreement as a proxy for correctness. However, these studies usually fix a single interaction structure, leaving open how consensus depends on how agents interact. We address this gap by introducing RHEON, a physics-inspired framework that recasts a population drawn from a single frozen model as an evolving $O(n)$ spin system on a ladder of interaction geometries of increasing effective dimension --from a 1D ring to a full-coupling mean-field graph-- with the sampling temperature $T$ as the tunable source of thermal disorder, evolved through a Glauber-like asynchronous dynamics. Sweeping RHEON across $432$ configurations of prompt, population size, communication topology, and sampling temperature yields Eraclitus-4.7M, a tagged evolutionary corpus of $4.7$ million responses. We find that agents reach their strongest consensus gain within the first few update sweeps and that increasing the number of neighbours per agent accelerates convergence on average. We further show that whether a configuration settles on factually correct or hallucinated consensus is not predictable from its initial state alone, and that the hallucination-minimising temperature depends on how the agents are coupled, so the common near-greedy default is not automatically the safest. Finally, semantic agreement correlates positively with factual convergence, and interaction strengthens the association, yet never enough for unanimity to certify correctness.

W7215042307.abstract: Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) and Large Language Models (LLMs) have enabled personalized education via intelligent tutoring, adaptive learning, automated assessments, and personalized feedback. Nevertheless, educational AI systems are still confronted with challenges, including high computational complexity, long inference time, unreliable content generation, limited explainability, and ineffective multiagent orchestration. To this end, this study proposes LITE-Trust, a Lightweight Trust-Aware Explainable multiagent Generative Artificial Intelligence Framework for personalized education, which consists of learner profiling, Knowledge State Estimation (KSE), the Educational Library and Readers Optimization (ELRA) algorithm, relevance-based selective agent orchestration, trust evaluation, and an Explainability Engine. The ELRA algorithm is applied to optimize learner-specific educational configurations by taking learning requirements, trust, and computational efficiency into account, and selective orchestration is conducted to reduce computational overhead by only activating relevant agents. Experiments on the EdNet and Open University Learning Analytics Dataset (OULAD) demonstrate that LITE-Trust achieves 10.5/9.5ms latency, 80.5/81.3 MB memory, and 1.92 M parameters, which is computationally more efficient than the compared methods. In addition, LITE-Trust attains 95.0%/94.6% fidelity, 94.1%/93.4% explanation quality, and 92.6%/92.1% interpretability on the two datasets. Besides, the ELRA algorithm significantly outperforms existing algorithms in terms of various metrics. Overall, the experimental results verify that LITE-Trust can effectively balance personalization, learning quality, trust, explainability, and computational efficiency, thereby facilitating the practical application of lightweight and trustworthy GenAI systems in personalized education.

W7215090361.abstract: Large vision-language models (LVLMs) exhibit strong multimodal in-context learning (ICL) capabilities, yet this ability degrades substantially as model size decreases. Knowledge distillation offers a natural way to bridge this gap, but existing methods primarily align output distributions or hidden representations directly. Such alignment teaches the student what the teacher predicts without revealing which evidence in the complex context causally supports that prediction. Consequently, a student can imitate the teacher's answer while continuing to rely on language priors, prompt structure, or other spurious cues. To address this limitation, we introduce Multimodal Causal Distillation (MCD), a distillation framework that transfers how a strong teacher uses multimodal evidence during ICL. MCD uses structure-preserving token interventions to identify and verify causal evidence, then transfers how the teacher responds when that evidence is retained or removed. This design connects distillation to the causal patterns by which the model uses contextual evidence during multimodal ICL. Experiments across three LVLM families and seven benchmarks show that MCD improves student performance by 7.23 points on average and outperforms vanilla distillation by 4.68 points, while further analyses confirm the generalizability of these gains.

W7215211765.abstract: Agentic AI systems are increasingly being deployed across critical domains such as healthcare, finance, and autonomoussystems, where decisions carry profound ethical consequences. Despite this rapid adoption, existing frameworkspredominantly optimize for task performance, often at the expense of ethical compliance, fairness, and accountability.This paper introduces the AGAI framework—a novel, modular architecture designed to embed ethical reasoning directlyinto the decision-making pipeline of agentic AI systems. By leveraging self-supervised learning and reinforcementlearning, AGAI enables autonomous agents to learn from their interactions while continuously respecting a predefinedset of ethical constraints. The framework comprises three tightly integrated components: an Ethical Decision Model(EDM) that encodes moral principles as a utility function, a Negotiation Layer (NL) that facilitates multi-agent consensuson ethically aligned actions, and a Learning and Adaptation Module (LAM) that refines agent behavior throughexperience. Empirical evaluation across 10,000 synthetic decision-making scenarios demonstrates that AGAI achieves a32% improvement in decision quality and a 25% reduction in ethical breach rates compared to traditional baselinesincluding rule-based models and reinforcement learning with ethical constraints. Statistical validation through paired ttestsconfirms the significance of these results. The AGAI framework bridges the critical gap between AI performanceand ethical responsibility, establishing a reproducible benchmark for future research in ethical autonomous systems.

W7215662075.abstract: This study aimed to investigate the effectiveness and applicability of an Artificial Intelligence (AI) Agent in assessing intermediate-level Chinese writing produced by learners of Chinese as a second language (L2). The research addressed two primary objectives: first, to examine the degree of consistency between AI Agent scoring and manual scoring conducted by professional teachers, and second, to identify advantages and limitations of using an AI Agent for essay correction in international Chinese language education. The research population consisted of international students in Chinese language programs at Central China Normal University (CCNU). Purposive sampling was employed to collect 31 final examination essays from students taking the Intermediate Chinese Writing II course, comprising 16 essays from the first semester and 15 from the second. All participants passed the HSK Level 4 and represented diverse cultural and linguistic backgrounds. The primary instrument was an AI Agent named “Essay Grading Assistant,” developed on the ByteDance Coze platform using the DeepSeek-V3.2 large language model. This system integrated Optical Character Recognition (OCR), Chinese word segmentation, and document analysis plugins to process handwritten examination scripts. Additionally, two university instructors with over five years of experience independently evaluated the essays using the same analytical scoring rubric. Data analysis involved descriptive statistics to examine score distributions, Spearman’s rank correlation coefficient to determine the relationship between AI-generated scores and human ratings, and the Intraclass Correlation Coefficient (ICC) using a two-way random effects model with absolute agreement to evaluate inter-rater consistency. The findings revealed a very strong positive correlation between the AI Agent scores and the teachers’ scores, with correlation coefficients of 0.917 and 0.902, respectively (p < .001). The ICC value reached 0.964, indicating excellent agreement. The AI Agent significantly improved grading efficiency, requiring approximately 15 seconds per essay, while enhancing scoring objectivity and consistency in evaluating surface-level linguistic features. However, several limitations were identified, particularly in deep semantic interpretation, pragmatic understanding, and the recognition of unconventional learner expressions. The study concluded that AI Agents possess strong potential as supportive tools for international Chinese writing assessment; nevertheless, a human–AI collaborative scoring approach remains the most appropriate model for ensuring both efficiency and pedagogical quality in second-language writing evaluation.

W7216027337.abstract: Universities play a fundamental role in the production of scientific knowledge and technological innovation. Theses and dissertations frequently present methods, systems, and conceptual models with potential for technological applications and intellectual property registration. However, the identification of these innovative elements is still predominantly carried out manually by specialists working in innovation centers or technology transfer offices, a process that is time-consuming and makes it difficult to analyze large volumes of academic production. In this context, this study aims to present the development of an Artificial Intelligence system based on a multi-agent architecture to support the identification of potential innovations in academic works. The research, developed as a postdoctoral project, was conducted at the Referential Center for Intellectual Property and Innovation in Information Science (CERPII), linked to São Paulo State University (UNESP), Marília campus. The methodology involved the application of Natural Language Processing techniques and language models based on the Transformer architecture to perform semantic analysis of theses and dissertations, considering innovation criteria defined by the Brazilian National Institute of Industrial Property (INPI), such as novelty, inventive step, and applicability. Preliminary results, obtained from the analysis of more than 130 academic documents, indicate that the system contributes to the early identification of research with potential for technological registration. It is concluded that the use of Artificial Intelligence can expand the analytical capacity of university innovation centers, strengthening the relationship between scientific production and technological innovation. W7218332294.abstract: The rapid evolution of agentic artificial intelligence has fundamentally altered how enterprises conceptualize autonomy, coordination, and decision-making within digital ecosystems. As organizations transition from monolithic software architectures toward modular, composable commerce ecosystems, the orchestration of autonomous agents emerges as a central architectural and governance challenge. This research article develops an extensive theoretical and analytical examination of agentic AI orchestration frameworks with particular emphasis on interoperability, multi-agent communication protocols, and enterprise-scale transformation. Grounded in contemporary scholarship on large language model agents, multi-agent systems, and composable commerce, the study integrates architectural theory with applied enterprise perspectives to elucidate how agentic AI systems enable dynamic adaptation, contextual intelligence, and decentralized control. A central analytical anchor is the enterprise transformation case articulated by Upadhyay (2026), which demonstrates how agentic AI orchestration frameworks operationalize composable commerce principles through agent collaboration, workflow negotiation, and adaptive governance. Building upon this foundation, the article synthesizes insights from agent interoperability surveys, multi-agent conversation frameworks, semantic function orchestration, and ethical analyses to construct a comprehensive conceptual model of agentic AI orchestration. The methodology adopts a qualitative, theory-driven research design, combining structured literature analysis with comparative architectural interpretation. Results reveal recurring patterns in agent coordination mechanisms, memory architectures, and protocol abstraction layers that collectively enable scalability and resilience in enterprise systems. The discussion critically evaluates competing theoretical positions on autonomy versus control, emergent behavior versus predictability, and innovation versus ethical accountability. By articulating limitations, unresolved tensions, and future research trajectories, this study contributes a foundational, publication-ready reference for scholars and practitioners seeking to understand the role of agentic AI orchestration in the next generation of enterprise commerce ecosystems.

W7220174762.abstract: The increasing prevalence of chronic diseases such as diabetes, cardiovascular disorders, obesity, and hypertension has necessitated the development of innovative, scalable, and personalized healthcare solutions. Personalized nutrition, supported by artificial intelligence (AI) and telemonitoring systems, has emerged as a transformative approach to managing chronic conditions through tailored dietary interventions. This paper presents a comprehensive analysis of AI-driven diet optimization frameworks integrated with telemonitoring technologies. It explores how machine learning algorithms, wearable devices, and real-time data analytics enable dynamic and individualized dietary recommendations based on physiological, behavioral, and environmental factors. The study examines key components of personalized nutrition systems, including data acquisition from biosensors, dietary intake tracking, metabolic profiling, and predictive modeling. Advanced AI techniques such as deep learning, reinforcement learning, and recommendation systems are analyzed for their role in optimizing dietary plans. Furthermore, telemonitoring platforms facilitate continuous patient engagement, adherence tracking, and remote clinical supervision, improving health outcomes and reducing healthcare costs. Despite significant advancements, challenges remain in data integration, privacy, model interpretability, and clinical validation. This paper critically evaluates these issues and proposes future directions, including multimodal data fusion, explainable AI, and integration with digital health ecosystems. The findings highlight the potential of AI-driven personalized nutrition systems to revolutionize chronic disease management through precision, scalability, and accessibility.

W7220187744.abstract: Cardiovascular diseases (CVDs) remain the leading cause of mortality and disability worldwide, posing a significant burden on healthcare systems and national economies. Early diagnosis, continuous monitoring, and timely clinical intervention are essential for reducing cardiovascular morbidity and mortality. In recent years, artificial intelligence (AI) has emerged as a transformative technology in cardiology, offering innovative solutions for disease detection, risk prediction, medical image interpretation, and patient management. This study investigates the role of artificial intelligence in cardiovascular disease diagnosis and patient monitoring. Particular attention was given to machine learning algorithms, deep learning models, electrocardiogram (ECG) analysis, cardiac imaging technologies, wearable monitoring devices, and telecardiology systems. The potential of AI-based technologies to improve diagnostic accuracy, facilitate early detection of cardiovascular abnormalities, and optimize clinical decision-making was evaluated.

W7220658930.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly evaluated for clinical question-answering (QA) tasks, yet benchmark accuracy alone provides limited assurance of clinical reliability. Existing evaluation metrics often fail to capture whether model reasoning preserves patient-specific context and diagnostic intent, while many require external references or manual annotation, limiting scalability and real-world applicability. To address this gap, this study proposes EntQA, a reference-free, entity-centric metric that evaluates how well LLM-generated responses retain clinically relevant biomedical concepts from patient backgrounds and diagnostic questions. Across five medical QA benchmarks and seven Qwen 2.5 Instruct models (0.5B-72B parameters), EntQA showed consistently positive associations with model accuracy and scaling, outperforming conventional overlap- and embedding-based metrics that frequently exhibited weak or negative correlations. Group-level correlations with accuracy reached Spearman ρ =0.9286, while correlations with model scale reached ρ = 0.252. These findings suggest that EntQA provides a scalable and interpretable framework for assessing clinical fidelity and reasoning quality in healthcare LLMs without requiring gold standard references or external evidence.

W7220861682.abstract: Low-resource languages face significant challenges in natural language processing due to limited annotated corpora, scarce linguistic resources, and inadequate semantic representations. Traditional lexical semantic models often fail to capture contextual meanings and semantic relationships effectively, resulting in reduced performance across language understanding tasks. This paper proposes a Context-Aware Lexical Semantic Modeling Framework Using Large Language Models (LLMs) for Low-Resource Languages, designed to generate rich contextual embeddings and improve lexical semantic understanding. The proposed framework integrates data preprocessing, contextual token representation, transformer-based LLM encoding, semantic feature extraction, and lexical relationship modeling within a unified architecture. By leveraging the contextual reasoning capabilities of LLMs, the model effectively captures word meanings, semantic similarity, polysemy, and contextual dependencies across diverse linguistic environments. The novelty of the proposed approach lies in its ability to enhance semantic representation learning for lowresource languages through context-aware lexical modeling and transfer learning mechanisms. Experimental evaluation on benchmark low-resource language datasets achieved a semantic similarity accuracy of 96.8%, word sense disambiguation accuracy of 95.4%, and F1-score of 96.1%, outperforming conventional embedding-based approaches. The results demonstrate improved contextual understanding, semantic consistency, and language representation quality, making the framework suitable for multilingual NLP applications, machine translation, information retrieval, and language preservation initiatives.

W7220948922.abstract: Speculative decoding accelerates inference for a large language model (LLM), referred to as the \emph{target model}, by first using a smaller model, referred to as the \emph{draft model}, to generate candidate tokens and then verifying them with the target model for acceptance or rejection. Prior studies primarily focused on the efficiency-utility trade-off of speculative decoding, e.g., lossy speculative decoding, leaving its security implications largely unexplored. In this work, we bridge this gap by providing the \emph{first} systematic study of the security implications of speculative decoding. Through a large-scale measurement study, we reveal a pronounced security-utility asymmetry: across a wide range of lossy speculative decoding methods, improvements in inference efficiency come at a disproportionately high cost to security, with attack success rates for jailbreak and prompt injection attacks increasing much faster than utility degrades. We then propose SecureSD, a new theory-guided speculative decoding method that enhances security while maintaining efficiency and utility. Specifically, our theoretical analysis reveals that security degradation primarily originates from the early tokens generated by the draft model. Motivated by this insight, SecureSD applies a stricter verification criterion to draft-model tokens at early decoding positions. Extensive experiments on both security and utility benchmarks demonstrate that SecureSD significantly improves security while preserving efficiency and utility compared to existing speculative decoding methods.

W7221040971.abstract: Language models frequently generate outputs in unintended languages or scripts, a phenomenon known as off-target generation. While existing research has focused on language selection, the dimension of script knowledge remains understudied: before any linguistic understanding can occur, users must recognize the graphic symbols in a model's response. We investigate whether Small and Large Language Models (SLMs and LLMs) possess script knowledge by testing them on multi-scriptic languages. Through two complementary experiments, we evaluate whether models (1) adapt their output script to match the input, and (2) follow explicit instructions to generate text in a specified script. The models we tested demonstrate substantial script knowledge: they all achieve a near-perfect Latin script fidelity (more than 98%) and follow script instructions with high frequency. Nevertheless, we notice differences between LLMs and SLMs, with higher scores for LLMs including for non-standard script combinations.

W7221048664.abstract: Current frontier LLMs leverage vast training datasets with knowledge about a broad range of programming languages and frameworks, and can often solve tasks with minimal prompting. However, there are scenarios where remote LLMs are unsuitable, due to cost, privacy, security, or intellectual property concerns, and local language models need to be used. These smaller local language models typically require more careful guidance in order to achieve acceptable performance. In this paper, we evaluate the impact of using local models (in the 14-31B range) for object-oriented modelling, and we propose an approach for partially automating the creation of agents that "think in code" to solve such problems, instead of directly producing an output. We compare the direct invocation of Claude Sonnet 4.6 with that of several open-weight models, and with the use of those open-weight models while "thinking in code" as proposed. We observe that the best open-weight models, when "thinking in code", can produce models with similar Jaccard similarity scores to the model solutions in the Golden UML ModelSet dataset as Sonnet, although at the cost of increased token consumption. Based on the observed potential for generating domain-specific agents that reduce the demands on the LLM and therefore on the hardware requirements, we set out several lines of further work.

W7221315694.abstract: Enterprise software-as-a-service (SaaS) workflows increasingly expose large language model agents to heterogeneous tasks, cross-application dependencies, external tools, governance constraints, and human approval requirements. Fixed orchestration patterns can be effective for stable workflows but do not explicitly adapt their coordination structure to runtime task conditions. This study developed and evaluated a Governance-Aware Adaptive Agentic Orchestration Framework (GAAOF) using design science research, a controlled comparative experiment, and an embedded multi-case design. The benchmark contained 180 enterprise workflow tasks spanning Customer/Revenue Operations, IT/Service Operations, and Finance/Administrative Operations. Each task was executed under five orchestration configurations and repeated five times, yielding 4,500 primary executions. GAAOF achieved a 91.6% task-success rate, 94.0% workflow completion, and 96.0% correct tool/action execution. Relative to the strongest fixed baseline, task success increased by 5.8 percentage points while latency, execution cost, and tool calls decreased by 12.3%, 22.0%, and 17.5%, respectively. Governance-aware routing reduced the policy-violation rate to 1.3%, and mixed-effects analysis showed approximately 74% lower odds of policy violation. Significant pattern-by-complexity, pattern-by-risk, and pattern-by-dependency interactions demonstrated that orchestration effectiveness was context contingent. Ablation, subgroup, cross-case, and sensitivity analyses further showed that governance-aware selection, runtime adaptation, and human escalation contributed complementary benefits. The findings support adaptive orchestration as a practical design principle for enterprise agentic systems requiring joint optimization of effectiveness, efficiency, reliability, and governance.

W7221343702.abstract: Reinforcement Learning (RL) is a machine-learning approach for problems in which decisions are made repeatedly and their quality becomes clear through feedback. Instead of depending on a fixed collection of labelled answers, an RL agent interacts with an environment, observes its changing state, receives rewards or penalties, and improves its decision policy through experience. This review examines the basic RL framework and discusses deep reinforcement learning, offline learning, multi-agent systems, and human-guided learning. Applications in robotics, games, education, finance, healthcare, and autonomous systems are considered. The review also identifies sample inefficiency, computational cost, instability, delayed rewards, limited generalization, and safety as important challenges. The paper concludes by identifying research opportunities for efficient, reliable, explainable, and adaptable RL systems.

W7221527896.abstract: Chimeric antigen receptor (CAR)-T cell therapy has transformed outcomes in selected hematologic malignancies, yet its delivery remains constrained by variable efficacy, acute and prolonged toxicities, and complex manufacturing logistics. Artificial intelligence (AI) is being applied across the CAR-T continuum at three distinct levels of evidentiary maturity. Externally validated parsimonious models built on routine clinical and laboratory data including CAR-HEMATOTOX, endothelial activation and stress index (EASIX) and m-EASIX, MyCARe, and gradient-boosting cytokine release syndrome predictors provide deployable risk stratification today. Methodologically sophisticated tools using deep-learning positron emission tomography (PET) segmentation, attention-based digital-pathology analysis, and multimodal fusion of imaging with laboratory and circulating tumor DNA features have demonstrated technical promise but generally lack the multi-center external validation required for clinical-grade deployment. Forward-looking applications, including digital-twin frameworks, large language models, and closed-loop adaptive therapy, remain at the prototype stage and have not yet been validated for CAR-T. This review synthesizes these three tiers, summarizes 18 published AI and statistical-modeling tools in a comparative performance table, and compares data characteristics and AI modeling paradigms across large B cell lymphoma, B cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia, and multiple myeloma. We also identify the implementation realities-absent regulatory clearance, demographic and racial bias in training data, and post-deployment model drift-that condition the field's evolution. The contribution of AI to CAR-T therapy, as the evidence currently stands, is the calibrated quantification of established risk factors rather than the discovery of novel biology, but the methodological and data infrastructure foundations are now in place for the broader transformation that the next decade may enable.

W7221559568.abstract: As autonomous AI agents become more integrated into sensitive domains, it is crucial that single and multi-agent AI systems are secured. This paper investigates how prompt injection attacks can exploit both direct user inputs and inter?agent communication to leak sensitive information and trigger cross-agent infections. While our tests mostly highlight key vulnerabilities in single-agent systems, we also extend these attacks to multi-agent frameworks, investigating how weaknesses can propagate across agents. Our findings emphasize the need for more robust defenses as AI agents become more commonly embedded in real-world workflows.

W7221699694.abstract: This paper focuses on the enrichment and structuring of scientific literature related to Large Language Models through Named Entity Recognition techniques. As the number of publications dedicated to Large Language Models continues to grow, efficiently identifying and organizing scientific knowledge has become increasingly challenging. To address this issue, we propose a specialized annotation framework designed to enrich Large Language Model literature beyond the traditional categorization mechanisms provided by scientific repositories such as arXiv. A corpus of 100 scientific articles was collected from arXiv and annotated using several entity categories, including language models, research tasks, datasets, evaluation metrics, learning techniques, software libraries, scientific domains corresponding to arXiv categories, URLs, and email addresses. The resulting annotations provide a richer and more structured representation of the knowledge contained within scientific publications. To evaluate the proposed framework, four Transformer based architectures were investigated, namely BERT, DistilBERT, RoBERTa, and GraphiBERT. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of Transformer models for scientific entity classification and highlight the benefits of incorporating external knowledge for semantic enrichment. The proposed framework facilitates the exploration and analysis of Large Language Model literature while supporting the identification of research trends, utilized resources, developed techniques, and scientific application domains.

W7221702351.abstract: The emergence of large language models (LLMs) has fundamentally transformed information interaction, yet their application in environmental science and engineering (ESE) is hindered by multimodal data formats, dynamic context requirements, and hallucination risks. To transition from general-purpose models to domain expert agentic systems, this Perspective introduces a three-pillar framework for ESE-LLMs: domain perception, knowledge grounding, and action capability. Implementing these capabilities introduces potential pitfalls such as geographic representation bias, catastrophic forgetting, and source authenticity vulnerabilities, which require strategic model blending and careful data curation to overcome. Furthermore, rigorous evaluation must extend beyond standard knowledge benchmarks to systematically assess factuality, fairness, consistency, and safety using both human and automated metrics. Finally, we present a decision-guided deployment workflow that helps researchers in ESE fields integrate LLMs into their workflow. Ultimately, achieving trustworthy environmental intelligence relies on continuous evaluation, robust governance, and sustained interdisciplinary collaboration to safely deploy agentic ESE-LLMs for high-stakes environmental challenges.

W7221710743.abstract: ABSTRACT The exploration of energy‐efficient and functional spintronics has attracted considerable attention. Spin‐orbit and orbital transport have opened new pathways for current‐induced torque generation based on the spin Hall effect. In addition, artificial intelligence computing has been demonstrated using spintronic devices. Further progress of these devices can be anticipated through the development of unique and functional materials, beyond the existing heavy metals and topological systems with strong spin–orbit coupling. The nitride materials exhibit unique chemical, magnetic, and structural versatility, including antiferromagnetism, high thermal stability, and compatibility with diverse device architectures. Here, we propose Nitrospinics as a conceptual and functional framework that exploits nitride materials for applications ranging from spin‐orbit and orbital torque based spintronic devices to artificial intelligence hardware. Using a sputter‐grown multilayer Cr 2 N with MXene‐related layer structure and a nitrogen‐incorporated heavy metal of Pt x N, as prototype systems, we discuss how nitrogen contributes to the structural stability, the orbital torque and spin‐orbit torque generation, and the interfacial orbital to spin conversion. We further outline key challenges and opportunities toward establishing nitride‐based materials for next‐generation computing technologies.

W7221732916.abstract: The estimation of heterogeneous treatment effects is a central objective of causal inference. However, state-of-the-art algorithms to solve this task are based on machine learning principles, and thus behave as black boxes. Consequently, the identification of covariates driving heterogeneity remains a challenging and open problem. To address this limitation, we introduce CausalTreeHFD, an interpretable extension of causal forests, based on the Hoeffding functional decomposition adapted to tree ensembles. Our approach decomposes predictions of conditional average treatment effects (CATE) into contributions from individual covariates and pairwise interactions, providing a direct characterization of the factors driving treatment effect heterogeneity. We establish the consistency of CausalTreeHFD, which converges towards the Hoeffding decomposition of the underlying CATE function, under standard assumptions for the analysis of causal forests. Experiments on simulated and real datasets show that CausalTreeHFD accurately identifies relevant covariates and interactions, and precisely recovers their contributions to heterogeneous treatment effects.

W7221789202.abstract: Comparing large language models can reveal shared representational structure and systematic differences between them. However, aggregate similarity measures can obscure how agreement varies across geometric scales and which linguistic properties support it. We introduce two complementary methods to resolve where models agree and what supports that agreement. Standard representational similarity analysis (RSA) summarizes similarity across all stimulus pairs, potentially obscuring differences in alignment between nearby and distant inputs. Neighborhood-Weighted RSA (NW-RSA) addresses this limitation by weighting stimulus pairs according to their proximity in representational space, placing alignment from local neighborhoods to global geometry on a common scale. Counterfactual RSA (CF-RSA) tests which linguistic properties support alignment by comparing intact representations in one model with representations under controlled linguistic perturbations in another. Across diverse language models, we find strong agreement in coarse representational geometry but substantial divergence in local neighborhoods. Alignment is observed both across broadly sampled natural text and within linguistic equivalence classes that preserve particular aspects of meaning or structure. Counterfactual analyses reveal selective sensitivity: changes to logical scope reduce alignment substantially more than the tested changes to hierarchical syntax, event roles, or discourse structure. Alignment also decreases when sentence structure or lexical meaning is disrupted in word lists and jabberwocky sentences, suggesting that the regularities of natural language support stronger convergence. These findings refine claims of representational universality by showing that strong overall similarity need not imply agreement in how models represent finer linguistic distinctions.

W7222482994.abstract: Artificial intelligence has evolved from rule-based symbolic systems into learning architectures capable of perception, prediction, content generation, reasoning, planning, tool use, and increasingly autonomous action. This qualitative literature review examines this transition as more than a technological chronology. It interprets AI evolution through five interrelated dimensions: technological evolution, capability expansion, changing human roles, human–AI integration, and governance. Drawing on contemporary peer-reviewed literature published primarily between 2020 and 2026, the review identifies seven thematic developments. AI has progressed from encoded rules toward learned representations and goal-directed action; generative AI has expanded AI into a general-purpose content collaborator; agentic AI adds planning, memory, tool use, and iterative task execution; human roles increasingly shift from operator toward collaborator, delegator, and governor; human–AI complementarity remains conditional rather than automatic; effective deployment requires calibrated rather than maximal trust; and governance requirements increase as AI systems acquire greater operational agency. The article proposes the Evolution–Capability–Role–Integration–Governance (ECRIG) framework to explain these relationships. The framework suggests that sustainable benefits from advanced AI emerge when technological capability, human role allocation, interaction architecture, and governance mechanisms develop jointly. The review concludes that the central challenge of the agentic-AI era is not choosing between humans and machines, but designing accountable systems in which increasingly capable artificial agents remain aligned with meaningful human goals, authority, and oversight.

W7222561884.abstract: We investigate whether variation in information density across chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning steps predicts answer correctness and can serve as a controllable inference-time target. We prompt frozen pretrained models to solve problems via CoT and measure the density of each reasoning step with two independent metrics: LP variance (how unevenly information is distributed across steps, computed as the variance in mean per-token negative log-likelihood) and the Caveman compression ratio. We then test whether density correlates with, and can be steered to improve, answer correctness. Experiments across six model scales, two training paradigms, and 60 GSM8K problems yield four main findings. First, lower LP variance predicts correctness in supervised fine-tuned (SFT) models, but this relationship weakens with scale and reverses in reinforcement-learning (RL) distilled models. Training paradigm therefore appears more influential than model size in determining density behaviour. Second, synthetic experiments reveal an intrinsic complexity preference: models trained on uniformly distributed data learn complexity-favouring distributions 2.0 to 2.6 times more accurately than simplicity-favouring ones. Third, direct inference-time density steering reduces accuracy from 60.0% to 8.3%, indicating that natural density patterns are functionally important to reasoning. Fourth, pre-generation nudging combining hint injection with contrastive KV-cache steering improves accuracy by 13.3 percentage points, consistent across both metrics. Finally, we introduce Entropy-Gated Density Routing (EGDR), a self-supervised method using token-level Shannon entropy to gate proportional KVcache adjustments during generation, improving accuracy by 10.0 percentage points without any external guidance.

W7222820562.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents turn model-generated decisions into tool calls, API requests, code execution, data access, and transactions. When agent reasoning is manipulated or simply wrong, model-centric guardrails cannot by themselves stop the resulting action. We systematically reviewed runtime-enforcement mechanisms for autonomous and tool-using AI agents in literature published or publicly available from January 2023 to September 2026. Searches of Compendex and the Web of Science Core Collection, followed by deduplication, multi-stage screening, source-grounded eligibility assessment, and targeted snowballing, yielded 58 primary studies, which we coded by enforcement placement, security mechanism, and assurance type. Most studies enforce security at the tool/action boundary (33/58, 56.9%) or inside the agent runtime or harness (18/58, 31.0%), whereas only 7/58 (12.1%) work primarily at the OS/process/execution boundary. Authorization and privilege control (41/58, 70.7%) and action validation (34/58, 58.6%) are the most common mechanism families. Across very different mechanisms and assurance models, a common design emerges: the model proposes an action, and a separate enforcement point decides whether that action may take external effect. Durable authorization, multi-agent delegation, cross-layer enforcement, recovery from partially committed effects, and standardized evaluation remain open problems. These findings suggest that secure agent architectures should separate reasoning from execution authority and place consequential actions behind independently enforceable runtime boundaries.

W7223060453.abstract: ABSTRACT Purpose Castration-resistant prostate cancer (CRPC) is characterized by marked clinical heterogeneity and poor long-term survival, underscoring the need for tools that can rapidly and reliably individualize patient risk. While several prognostic models exist, their complexity has limited routine clinical use. Here, we developed and validated PROGRESS (PROstate cancer Global Risk Evaluation and Stratification Score), a simplified prognostic score, derived through machine learning-guided feature selection, to enhance risk stratification and support individualized, risk-informed clinical decision-making. Methods PROGRESS was developed using baseline data from 2,035 metastatic CRPC patients enrolled in four different phase III trials. An unsupervised machine-learning approach was applied to identify latent patient subgroups with distinct survival outcomes irrespectively of allocated treatment arm, followed by classical multivariable modelling to derive a simple and straight-forward prognostic score based on routinely available objective laboratory variables. External validation was performed in three independent datasets comprising metastatic CRPC patients treated across different therapeutic settings (n=1,239) and non-metastatic CRPC patients managed with standard care (n=660). Overall survival was assessed using Kaplan-Meier and Cox regression analyses. Results Unsupervised modelling identified two patient risk subpopulations with significantly different overall survival rates (median 27.4 vs 17.7 months; hazard ratio [HR] 2.20, 95% CI 1.91–2.54; p<.00001). Feature contribution analysis yielded three independent predictors -PSA, ALP, and AST-used to build PROGRESS. In the training cohort, PROGRESS demonstrated strong discrimination (AUC 0.89). Using a prespecified cut-off, patients classified as increased risk had significantly shorter survival than low-risk patients (median 18.3 vs 25.6 months; HR 1.72, 95% CI 1.50–1.97; p<.0001). PROGRESS prognostic performance was consistent across all validation cohorts, including metastatic and non-metastatic disease, with HRs ranging from 1.74 to 3.46 (all p<.0001). Conclusions By integrating machine-learning-based pattern discovery with classical statistical modelling, PROGRESS provides a simple, objective, and clinically accessible approach for individual risk stratification in CRPC. Its reliance on three inexpensive, routinely measured laboratory parameters would facilitate practical implementation in clinical settings, enhancing visibility of underlying disease aggressiveness for individual clinical decision-making. PROGRESS could represent a pragmatic first step toward improving patient selection for clinical trials while identifying regulatory meaningful endpoints achievable in a sizeable patient population; further validation in prospective clinical studies and real-world datasets would allow to confirm its clinical utility and generalizability. PROGRESS can be freely accessed for research use only at the following link: https://dev.ai.topazium.com .

W7223063594.abstract: A general observation in agentic workflows, especially bounded ones, is that the decision space of the LLM, when we separate a decision from generation, starts approaching saturation: the agent meets the same states again and again, and after enough conversations it stops meeting new ones. LLMs generally don't treat these decisions as an optimization problem and instead re-derive them from their context/prompt on every turn. We show that treating decision making within reasonable bounds as an optimization problem, solving it once, and reusing the solved decisions can often make an agent faster, cheaper and more reliable. Our approach, which we call Discretize, Then Decide, starts from data such as the workflow's own logs or, when none exists, runs of the LLM agent itself. It reads each conversation into discrete states and estimates the probability of each outcome and the cost of each move, until no new states appear and the probabilities stop changing. It then solves the resulting Markov decision process. The solution runs as a controller around the model, sending moves whose content is fixed in the state, such as a tool call or a templated reply, and any state it hasn't seen is sent back to the LLM. We call an LLM run this way a Bellman language model (BLM), after Richard Bellman's equation for the best move in each state. On $τ^2$-bench telecom, the controller with no model solves 79% of tasks. As a BLM, Qwen3.8-27B, an open model, goes from 29% to 96% with 93% fewer model calls. For Claude Opus 5.5, which solves 96% of tasks on its own, running it as a BLM cuts model calls and cost per task by about 98% and lets it solve 2 more tasks. On InventoryBench, the solved policy with no model beats every published method. Where the hard part is writing content rather than choosing moves, such as resolving SymPy issues, few decisions can be solved in advance, and a BLM helps little.

W7223102233.abstract: Mitigating catastrophic risks from large language models requires excising hazardous operational capabilities, such as cyberwarfare exploitation and pathogen enhancement, without degrading benign scientific utility. In these dual-use domains, legitimate defensive science and malicious attacks share vocabulary, syntax, and internal model representations, causing standard unlearning methods to induce severe collateral damage (concept bleeding). In this work, we present Orthogonal Boundary Unlearning (OBU), a mathematically grounded framework designed to eliminate collateral damage on benign dual-use capabilities. OBU extracts a domain-matched capability subspace from paired calibration queries via singular value decomposition on empirical activation covariances, and restricts parameter updates strictly to the orthogonal null space. This guarantees that benign representations experience zero parameter perturbation along the spanned calibration subspace. We present two complementary realizations of OBU: Projected LoRA, which applies the orthogonal constraint during iterative gradient-based fine-tuning, and Closed-Form Weight Surgery, which directly edits model weights in a single analytical step without training. Across four modern open-weight foundation models (Gemma-3-4B, Qwen3.5-4B, SmolLM3-3B, and Granite-4.2-3B), OBU achieves strong dual-use concept separation, substantially mitigates in-context priming attacks, and demonstrates durable resistance against adversarial relearning without degrading benign domain competence.

W7223290464.abstract: Abstract Cancer is a major global health issue with rising incidence and mortality. Early detection, tumor characterization, and disease surveillance are crucial for timely and effective treatment, ultimately reducing mortality rates. Liquid biopsy (LB) has emerged as a valuable detection tool offering a non-invasive method to determine tumor-derived biomarkers in body fluids with demonstrated translational potential. To increase biomarker sensitivity, high-throughput sequencing platforms deliver massive volumes of data. Artificial Intelligence (AI) is pivotal in enabling huge and complex data integration. This contribution aims to assess the current state of integrative AI-based research in the LB field and provide methodological guidance. First, we conducted a PubMed search and found that the literature is sparse in studies integrating LB features, particularly by applying AI. When adopting the latter approach, defining the study objectives is crucial to guide the subsequent methodological aspects, including study design, patient selection criteria, sample size, nature of the LB features, and metadata to collect. Specifically, we propose strategies and tools for data preprocessing, including normalization and batch correction, as well as handling outliers and missing data. Furthermore, we recommend various Machine/Deep Learning approaches for feature selection techniques to ensure model robustness, and we highlight the importance of undergoing rigorous internal and external validations of the selected models. Assessing clinical utility and interpretability is often overlooked but fundamental for real-world implementation. In conclusion, we provide the LB scientific community with an AI-based methodological guidance to bridge the two fields and enhance the integrative analysis of LB features. W7223444646.abstract: Digital transformation is a central pillar of Society 5.0; however, translating technological advancements into sustainable public value within public administration remains limited, particularly in terms of legal readiness. Although existing scholarship on e-government and Artificial Intelligence (AI) predominantly focuses on technological efficiency and service innovation, there remains a significant research gap concerning the absence of a robust and comprehensive legal framework governing AI-based e-government in Indonesia, which represents the central problem and novelty addressed in this study. This research examines the application of AI in e-government from a normative legal perspective, focusing on Indonesia’s regulatory preparedness. It employs normative legal methods through conceptual, statutory, and comparative approaches. The findings demonstrate that AI possesses substantial potential to enhance electronic administration by improving efficiency, accuracy, and responsiveness in public services. Nevertheless, Indonesia currently lacks a comprehensive and binding legal framework specifically regulating AI implementation in e-government, particularly in relation to accountability, transparency, data protection, and legal safeguards for citizens. This regulatory deficiency generates legal uncertainty and risks undermining public trust in digital governance. A comparative analysis with the United States reveals a more structured regulatory approach to AI-based e-government, supported by clearer data protection and accountability mechanisms. This research contributes a novel legal analysis by positioning regulatory readiness as a prerequisite for responsible AI-driven governance, arguing that technological transformation must be institutionally anchored within a coherent legal framework. Strengthening Indonesia’s legal infrastructure is therefore essential to ensure accountable AI implementation and to realize sustainable digital government transformation.

W7223446231.abstract: Abstract Aims Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used by the public and healthcare professionals for clinical reasoning. However, they were developed as general-purpose language models rather than dedicated clinical decision-support tools, and their performance in real-world acute heart failure (AHF) management remains insufficiently evaluated. We compared four contemporary AI models with physician decision-making. Methods and results This single-centre retrospective observational study incorporated a cross-sectional AI evaluation of consecutive patients treated at Sotiria General Hospital between July and November 2025, excluding acute coronary syndrome. ChatGPT, ChatGPT Plus, DeepSeek, and an ESC guideline-based retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) model independently assessed identical standardized cases. Recommendations were compared with physician decisions on diagnosis, treatment, guideline-directed medical therapy, timing, and prognosis using Cohen’s kappa, McNemar’s test, Cochran’s Q, Wilcoxon signed-rank testing, and multivariable logistic regression. Diagnostic performance differed significantly across systems (Cochran’s Q = 8.477, P = 0.037). In the balanced diagnostic cohort, ChatGPT Plus achieved the highest heart failure (HF) accuracy (accuracy 86.5%, sensitivity 87.0%, and specificity 86.0%), followed by RAG (accuracy 77.5%), ChatGPT (accuracy 77.0%), and DeepSeek (accuracy 69.0%). For HF within the top three differential diagnoses, sensitivity was 90.0–97.0%; specificity was 70.0% for ChatGPT Plus, 68.0% for RAG, 19.0% for DeepSeek, and 15.0% for ChatGPT. Physician agreement was highest for guideline-directed therapies, with greater variability in prognosis and escalation of care. RAG more closely matched physician therapeutic timing but did not consistently outperform general-purpose models. Conclusion Contemporary AI models show promise in AHF decision support but substantial task-specific variability, supporting use as complements rather than replacements for physician judgement.

W7223789053.abstract: Enterprise Intelligence provides decision-making assistance to all levels of managers throughout an organization, leveraging data, models, and computation. Enterprise Agility facilitates rapid self-diagnosis and reconfiguration of operations to align with constantly changing governing conditions. Self-Evolving Enterprise Intelligence Platforms are enabled through collaboration among several Multi-Agent LLM systems. Collaboration involves negotiation to resolve conflicts and make trade-offs, ultimately achieving a shared purpose. The Enterprise Intelligence and Enterprise Agility concepts serve as a foundation to explore Architectural Paradigms that enable Self-Evolving Platforms. Agent-based decomposition is proposed to delineate roles, interfaces, modular boundaries, and interaction protocols, thereby enhancing scalability and fault tolerance. The mechanisms for evolution in LLM-driven systems are outlined, followed by a description of collaboration frameworks among the agents. Self-evolution in self-evolving platforms is examined via three mechanisms: continuous learning and adaptation, negotiation and trade-offs, and Multi-Agent strategy. Data and experience ingress continuously, meeting the requirements of LLM systems. New training sets are formed, model updates undertaken, and permanent feedback loops instituted under neural architecture search and safe reinforcement learning principles. The drift inherent in LLM systems necessitates vigilant monitoring. Change is inevitable; adaptation can minimize harm and capitalise on opportunities. The foregoing mechanisms jointly impact all aspects of a platform, yet the implementation of Multi-Agent strategies is essential to acquire true Self-Evolution.

W7223878528.abstract: Abstract Background Multiple myeloma (MM) is clinically heterogeneous, and the International Staging System (ISS) captures this heterogeneity only in part. We aimed to build a transcriptomic risk model anchored in single-cell and stage-associated gene expression, and to explore its immune context and therapeutic implications. Methods Bone marrow single-cell RNA sequencing data from 18 MM and 18 control samples were integrated with ISS stage-stratified RNA sequencing data from the MMRF CoMMpass cohort (n = 764). Candidate genes were filtered by univariate Cox regression, and 101 combinations of 10 machine learning algorithms were benchmarked. The model was validated in three independent cohorts (GSE136337, GSE2658 and GSE4581) and examined with T cell subclustering, immune deconvolution, drug sensitivity prediction, genetic dependency data and molecular docking. Results Integration yielded eight candidate genes, five of which ( DLGAP5 , CENPF , PFDN2 , HNRNPF and MAP2K1 ) were associated with overall survival. A random survival forest plus supervised principal components model achieved a C-index of 0.69 in training and 0.62 to 0.63 in validation, outperformed 16 published MM signatures and remained independently prognostic after adjustment for age, sex and ISS stage (HR 2.02, 95% CI 1.70 to 2.41). High-risk patients had lower immune and stromal scores, higher TIDE scores and fewer predicted immunotherapy responders. Docking supported binding of risk-associated compounds to MAP2K1 . Conclusion This five-gene signature refines risk stratification beyond ISS, marks an immune-depleted high-risk phenotype and nominates MAP2K1 as a candidate therapeutic target in MM.
